stories.title: Jonah Flees and Is Swallowed
stories.keyVerse: "So they took up Jonah, and cast him forth into the sea: and the sea ceased from her raging."
stories.text:
Now the word of the LORD came unto Jonah the son of Amittai, saying,
Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and cry against it; for their wickedness is come up before me.
But Jonah rose up to flee unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD, and went down to Joppa; and he found a ship going to Tarshish: so he paid the fare thereof, and went down into it, to go with them unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD.
But the LORD sent out a great wind into the sea, and there was a mighty tempest in the sea, so that the ship was like to be broken.
Then the mariners were afraid, and cried every man unto his god, and cast forth the wares that
were in the ship into the sea, to lighten
it of them. But Jonah was gone down into the sides of the ship; and he lay, and was fast asleep.
So the shipmaster came to him, and said unto him, What meanest thou, O sleeper? arise, call upon thy God, if so be that God will think upon us, that we perish not.
And they said every one to his fellow, Come, and let us cast lots, that we may know for whose cause this evil
is upon us. So they cast lots, and the lot fell upon Jonah.
Then said they unto him, Tell us, we pray thee, for whose cause this evil
is upon us; What
is thine occupation? and whence comest thou? what
is thy country? and of what people
art thou?
And he said unto them, I
am an Hebrew; and I fear the LORD, the God of heaven, which hath made the sea and the dry
land.
Then were the men exceedingly afraid, and said unto him, Why hast thou done this? For the men knew that he fled from the presence of the LORD, because he had told them.
Then said they unto him, What shall we do unto thee, that the sea may be calm unto us? for the sea wrought, and was tempestuous.
And he said unto them, Take me up, and cast me forth into the sea; so shall the sea be calm unto you: for I know that for my sake this great tempest
is upon you.
Nevertheless the men rowed hard to bring
it to the land; but they could not: for the sea wrought, and was tempestuous against them.
Wherefore they cried unto the LORD, and said, We beseech thee, O LORD, we beseech thee, let us not perish for this man’s life, and lay not upon us innocent blood: for thou, O LORD, hast done as it pleased thee.
So they took up Jonah, and cast him forth into the sea: and the sea ceased from her raging.
Then the men feared the LORD exceedingly, and offered a sacrifice unto the LORD, and made vows.
Now the LORD had prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah. And Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights.
Then Jonah prayed unto the LORD his God out of the fish’s belly,
And said, I cried by reason of mine affliction unto the LORD, and he heard me; out of the belly of hell cried I,
and thou heardest my voice.
For thou hadst cast me into the deep, in the midst of the seas; and the floods compassed me about: all thy billows and thy waves passed over me.
Then I said, I am cast out of thy sight; yet I will look again toward thy holy temple.
The waters compassed me about,
even to the soul: the depth closed me round about, the weeds were wrapped about my head.
I went down to the bottoms of the mountains; the earth with her bars
was about me for ever: yet hast thou brought up my life from corruption, O LORD my God.
When my soul fainted within me I remembered the LORD: and my prayer came in unto thee, into thine holy temple.
They that observe lying vanities forsake their own mercy.
But I will sacrifice unto thee with the voice of thanksgiving; I will pay
that that I have vowed. Salvation
is of the LORD.
And the LORD spake unto the fish, and it vomited out Jonah upon the dry
land.
stories.retelling:
The word of God came to Jonah, a prophet living in the sun-baked streets of Israel. He was tasked with a daunting mission: **"Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and cry against it; for their wickedness is come up before me."** But the thought of facing Nineveh's infamous brutality filled Jonah with dread. Instead of heading east, he packed his belongings and fled west, toward the port city of Joppa. There, he found a ship bound for Tarshish, far from the prying eyes of God.

As the ship set sail, Jonah descended into its depths, hoping to find solace in sleep. Above him, the sky darkened and the wind began to howl. The ocean churned violently, and a monstrous storm erupted, threatening to tear the vessel apart. The sailors, seasoned and rugged, were seized by terror. Desperately, they tossed their cargo overboard, hoping to keep the ship afloat.

Amidst the chaos, the ship's captain discovered Jonah asleep and shook him awake. **"What meanest thou, O sleeper?"** he cried. **"Arise, call upon thy God."** The crew, fearing divine wrath, decided to cast lots to determine who was responsible for their plight. As the lots were drawn, Jonah's name emerged, sealing his fate.

Confronted by the anxious sailors, Jonah admitted, **"I am a Hebrew; and I fear the LORD, the God of heaven, which hath made the sea and the dry land."** Realizing that Jonah was fleeing from God, the men were aghast. They demanded to know what they should do to calm the raging sea.

Jonah, resigned and burdened by guilt, instructed them, **"Take me up, and cast me forth into the sea; so shall the sea be calm unto you."** Reluctantly, the men attempted to row back to land, but the storm only grew fiercer. In a final act of desperation, they cried out, **"We beseech thee, O LORD, we beseech thee, let us not perish for this man’s life."**

With no other choice, they lifted Jonah and cast him into the frothing abyss. Instantly, the sea calmed, its rage subsiding into a serene, glassy surface. The sailors, awestruck by the miracle, offered sacrifices and made vows to God, their hearts filled with reverent fear.

Beneath the waves, Jonah was enveloped by darkness as a massive fish, prepared by the Lord, swallowed him whole. For three days and nights, Jonah languished in the creature’s belly, engulfed by despair and isolation. Amidst the dank confines, he prayed, acknowledging his plight: **"I cried by reason of mine affliction unto the LORD, and he heard me."**

Finally, God commanded the fish, and it released Jonah onto dry land, delivering him back to the world with a renewed sense of purpose and humility. As he lay on the shore, drenched and gasping for breath, he understood the weight of his calling and the mercy of the God he served.

stories.title: Nineveh Repents
stories.keyVerse: "Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown."
stories.text:
And the word of the LORD came unto Jonah the second time, saying,
Arise, go unto Nineveh, that great city, and preach unto it the preaching that I bid thee.
So Jonah arose, and went unto Nineveh, according to the word of the LORD. Now Nineveh was an exceeding great city of three days’ journey.
And Jonah began to enter into the city a day’s journey, and he cried, and said, Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown.
So the people of Nineveh believed God, and proclaimed a fast, and put on sackcloth, from the greatest of them even to the least of them.
For word came unto the king of Nineveh, and he arose from his throne, and he laid his robe from him, and covered
him with sackcloth, and sat in ashes.
And he caused
it to be proclaimed and published through Nineveh by the decree of the king and his nobles, saying, Let neither man nor beast, herd nor flock, taste any thing: let them not feed, nor drink water:
But let man and beast be covered with sackcloth, and cry mightily unto God: yea, let them turn every one from his evil way, and from the violence that
is in their hands.
Who can tell
if God will turn and repent, and turn away from his fierce anger, that we perish not?
And God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way; and God repented of the evil, that he had said that he would do unto them; and he did
it not.
But it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was very angry.
And he prayed unto the LORD, and said, I pray thee, O LORD,
was
not this my saying, when I was yet in my country? Therefore I fled before unto Tarshish: for I knew that thou
art a gracious God, and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and repentest thee of the evil.
Therefore now, O LORD, take, I beseech thee, my life from me; for
it is better for me to die than to live.
Then said the LORD, Doest thou well to be angry?
So Jonah went out of the city, and sat on the east side of the city, and there made him a booth, and sat under it in the shadow, till he might see what would become of the city.
And the LORD God prepared a gourd, and made
it to come up over Jonah, that it might be a shadow over his head, to deliver him from his grief. So Jonah was exceeding glad of the gourd.
But God prepared a worm when the morning rose the next day, and it smote the gourd that it withered.
And it came to pass, when the sun did arise, that God prepared a vehement east wind; and the sun beat upon the head of Jonah, that he fainted, and wished in himself to die, and said,
It is better for me to die than to live.
And God said to Jonah, Doest thou well to be angry for the gourd? And he said, I do well to be angry,
even unto death.
Then said the LORD, Thou hast had pity on the gourd, for the which thou hast not laboured, neither madest it grow; which came up in a night, and perished in a night:
And should not I spare Nineveh, that great city, wherein are more than sixscore thousand persons that cannot discern between their right hand and their left hand; and
also much cattle?
stories.retelling:
The morning air was filled with anticipation as Jonah, a solitary figure against the vastness of the landscape, approached the sprawling city of Nineveh. The city was a behemoth, stretching for miles and bustling with life. Its walls loomed tall, an imposing testament to its greatness, and the streets were alive with the hum of daily activity.

Jonah, with resolve in his eyes, entered the city. Each step echoed with the weight of his mission. He walked a full day, feeling the curious gazes of the townspeople upon him. At last, he stopped, his voice rising above the din of the crowded streets. **"Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown,"** he declared, each word resonating with urgency.

The message spread like wildfire, reaching ears that listened and hearts that stirred. The people of Nineveh, from merchants to laborers, recognized the gravity of Jonah's proclamation. They halted their daily routines, their faces etched with concern. A collective decision swept through the city; they would fast. Sackcloth replaced fine garments, a symbol of humility and repentance.

As the news reached the king, he too was moved. The opulence of his throne room felt hollow as he rose, discarding his royal robe. Clad in sackcloth, he sat in ashes, a poignant image of a ruler's vulnerability before the divine. He issued a decree throughout Nineveh, commanding all—humans and animals alike—to neither eat nor drink. The city, once vibrant, was now a place of solemn reflection. The king urged his people to abandon their violent ways, to seek mercy with fervent prayers. **"Who can tell if God will turn and repent?"** he pondered, hope mingling with fear.

God observed Nineveh's transformation, noting their genuine shift from wickedness. In His compassion, He decided not to bring the destruction He had warned of. The city was spared.

Yet, outside the city, Jonah's heart was not at ease. Anger simmered within him, for he had hoped to witness the city's downfall. He prayed, his words tinged with frustration. **"I knew that thou art a gracious God,"** he lamented, his voice a mix of resignation and bitterness. Seeking solace, Jonah retreated to the east of the city, constructing a makeshift shelter to watch the unfolding events.

God, in His wisdom, orchestrated a lesson. A vine grew overnight, its broad leaves casting a comforting shade over Jonah. Grateful, Jonah's spirits lifted. But by dawn, a worm gnawed at the vine, and it withered. The sun rose mercilessly, and a scorching wind blasted Jonah, leaving him faint and despondent. **"It is better for me to die than to live,"** he muttered, the heat intensifying his despair.

God questioned Jonah's anger over the vine, drawing a parallel to His own concern for Nineveh. **"Should not I spare Nineveh,"** He asked, highlighting the value of the lives within the city compared to the fleeting vine. In the end, the lesson was clear: compassion and mercy extend beyond human understanding.
